title: All Call: What Are You Woodenizing Right Now?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. responds to a reader's suggestion to open the school year with an "all call" for what teachers are "Woodenizing," his term, named for legendary basketball coach John Wooden's famous practice of teaching college athletes to properly put on socks and tie shoes on day one, for the discipline of assuming that if you want students to do something well, it is the teacher's job to be explicitly clear about how to do it. He organizes Woodenizing targets into two categories: "Smallies," habit-level routines that can be taught once with total clarity and then reinforced calmly and consistently (entering the classroom, finding assignments on Canvas, using a cell-phone garage), and "Biggies," skill-level practices that require repeated teaching, modeling, and time to develop (note-taking, writing stamina, effective studying). The piece frames the key planning question as: what learning-conducive behaviors do I want every student to master, then pick a few smallies and one biggie and break them down with maximum clarity. Stuart offers his own current Woodenizing targets, note-taking for learning and building retrieval practice into classwork and homework, as a model before opening the question to readers.
points: Woodenization's origin story, Coach John Wooden explicitly teaching college athletes to put on socks and tie shoes correctly on the first day of practice, reframes 'over-explaining' basics not as condescension but as the teacher's responsibility whenever a behavior matters to later performance.

The Smallies/Biggies distinction gives teachers a planning heuristic that separates habit-level routines (taught once, then reinforced 'calmly and religiously') from skill-level competencies (requiring repeated teaching, modeling, and time), preventing teachers from treating both the same way.

The core diagnostic question, 'what learning-conducive behaviors would I like all of my students to master?', reframes classroom routines and skills as a deliberate, prioritized short list rather than an implicit assumption that students already know how to do things because they've 'encountered them in school before.'

Stuart's own worked example, treating 'how to handle the names of texts in writing' as a smallie whose success depends on reinforcement quality rather than the initial teaching, models how to sort a specific classroom problem into the framework's two categories.
quotes: Woodenization is first and foremost an attitude that says, I assume that if I want my students to do something well, it's my job to be clear about how to do it.
The name comes from Coach John Wooden, who famously taught his collegiate athletes how to put on their socks and tie their shoes on the first day of practice each season.
When Woodenizing, teachers are wise to think in terms of two categories: Smallies, stuff that can be taught once, with total clarity, and then reinforced thereafter. Smallies are matters of habit.
Biggies, stuff that needs to be taught multiple times over a time period in order for students to better understand how to do it well. Biggies are matters of skill.

The key question of the Woodenizer is: what learning-conducive behaviors would I like all of my students to master? From there, pick a few smallies and one biggie that you most want your students to master, and start breaking them down with as much clarity and simplicity and power as you can.
